f<sub>SR</sub> ≈ 1/(2π√(LC<sub>p</sub>)); above it an inductor is capacitive.
C(V<sub>R</sub>) = C<sub>j0</sub>/(1 + V<sub>R</sub>/φ)<sup>γ</sup>; tank frequency range = √(C<sub>max</sub>/C<sub>min</sub>).

F = F₁ + (F₂ − 1)/G₁ + (F₃ − 1)/(G₁G₂) + …, all linear.
P<sub>min</sub> = −174 + 10 log₁₀B + NF + SNR<sub>min</sub> dBm.
Input where output is 1 dB below the straight line; P1dB,out = P1dB,in + G − 1.
Intercept of the slope-1 and slope-3 lines; IIP3 = P<sub>in</sub> + ΔP/2; OIP3 = IIP3 + G.
1/IIP3 = 1/IIP3₁ + G₁/IIP3₂ + G₁G₂/IIP3₃ (mW, linear gains).
(2/3)(IIP3 − N), N the input noise floor in dBm.
f<sub>si</sub> = 2f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>RF</sub>, 2f<sub>IF</sub> from the signal.
α = √(1 + Q²ρ²), ρ = f<sub>si</sub>/f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>s</sub>/f<sub>si</sub>.
IRR ≈ 4/(ε² + θ²) for gain error ε and phase error θ (rad).
P<sub>PA</sub> − L<sub>feed</sub> + G<sub>ant</sub> (dBm).
Wanted-channel power ÷ adjacent-channel power, in dB; larger is better.
Re Z<sub>in</sub> = ω<sub>T</sub>L<sub>s</sub>; (L<sub>g</sub> + L<sub>s</sub>)C<sub>gs</sub> = 1/ω₀².
F = F<sub>min</sub> + (4R<sub>n</sub>/Z₀)|Γ<sub>s</sub> − Γ<sub>opt</sub>|²/[(1 − |Γ<sub>s</sub>|²)|1 + Γ<sub>opt</sub>|²].
P<sub>IF</sub>/P<sub>RF</sub>; ideal switching mixer 2/π (−3.9 dB); Gilbert cell (2/π)g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>L</sub>.
Input f with |m·f<sub>LO</sub> ± n·f| = f<sub>IF</sub>; half-IF spur at f<sub>RF</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub>/2 (high-side LO).
η<sub>D</sub> = P<sub>out</sub>/P<sub>DC</sub>; PAE = (P<sub>out</sub> − P<sub>in</sub>)/P<sub>DC</sub>.
R<sub>opt</sub> = 2(V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>knee</sub>)/I<sub>max</sub>; P<sub>out</sub> = (V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>knee</sub>)I<sub>max</sub>/4.
L(Δf) = 10 log₁₀[(2FkT/P<sub>s</sub>)(1 + (f₀/2QΔf)²)(1 + f<sub>c</sub>/Δf)] dBc/Hz.
f<sub>out</sub> = N·f<sub>ref</sub>; in-band noise = reference + 20 log₁₀N.

takeaways: A spiral inductor's real Q falls to zero at self-resonance: the 2 nH, 1 pF example has Q = 4.25 at 2 GHz, not the 6.28 of ωL/R<sub>s</sub>.
A varactor's capacitance ratio tunes a tank by only its square root: 2.26 in capacitance gives 1.50 in frequency.
Noise figures cascade by Friis in linear units; the first stage with gain sets most of the total, and any loss in front of it adds dB for dB.
Sensitivity is −174 dBm/Hz + 10 log₁₀B + NF + SNR<sub>min</sub>; every factor of 10 in bandwidth costs 10 dB.
Intercepts cascade the other way: later stages, seen after gain, usually limit IIP3, so LNA gain trades noise against linearity.
The image sits 2f<sub>IF</sub> from the signal and must be removed before the mixer, by filtering (α = √(1 + Q²ρ²)) or by I/Q cancellation (IRR ≈ 4/(ε² + θ²)).
In a transceiver the duplexer's loss counts on both paths, and its isolation must keep the transmit carrier and transmit noise out of the receiver.
An inductively degenerated LNA gets its 50 Ω from ω<sub>T</sub>L<sub>s</sub> with no resistor; the noise match and power match are close but not equal.
PA efficiency falls with back-off, Class A as the power ratio and Class B as the amplitude ratio; Doherty, envelope tracking and DPD win it back.
A PLL output follows the reference raised by 20 log₁₀N inside the loop and the free VCO outside it; the best loop bandwidth is where the two cross.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for a block diagram with the defining formula and units, then a numerical cascade or frequency plan, so every long answer below draws the chain, works the numbers and closes with a check.

bank.q: Define noise factor, noise figure and noise temperature. Write the Friis formula for three stages, explain why the first stage dominates, and write the sensitivity equation. Illustrate with an LNA (NF 1.5 dB, G 18 dB), a mixer (NF 10 dB, G 8 dB) and an IF stage (NF 15 dB) in a 200 kHz channel needing 9 dB SNR.
outline: F = SNR<sub>in</sub>/SNR<sub>out</sub> at 290 K, NF = 10 log₁₀F, T<sub>e</sub> = (F − 1)T₀
later stages divided by the gain ahead of them
example: F = 1.632, NF = 2.13 dB, P<sub>min</sub> = −109.9 dBm
answer: Noise factor: F = SNR<sub>in</sub>/SNR<sub>out</sub>, both power ratios in the same bandwidth with the source at T₀ = 290 K. It is a plain number, at least 1, because a real block adds noise of its own.

Noise figure: the same quantity in decibels, NF = 10 log₁₀F. Noise temperature: the temperature of a resistor that, placed at the input of a noiseless copy of the block, would give the same output noise: T<sub>e</sub> = (F − 1)T₀, so F = 1 + T<sub>e</sub>/T₀.
Friis formula for three stages, with every F and G as a linear ratio: F = F₁ + (F₂ − 1)/G₁ + (F₃ − 1)/(G₁G₂). In kelvin: T<sub>e</sub> = T<sub>e1</sub> + T<sub>e2</sub>/G₁ + T<sub>e3</sub>/(G₁G₂).

Why the first stage dominates: referred to the input, the noise a later stage adds is divided by the gain ahead of it, because the signal has already been amplified by that gain. With G₁ large the later terms shrink and F ≈ F₁. A passive loss L first has G = 1/L < 1, so it multiplies the later terms instead and adds its loss in dB to the total.
Sensitivity: P<sub>min</sub> = −174 + 10 log₁₀B + NF + SNR<sub>min</sub> dBm, where −174 dBm/Hz is kT₀, B is the channel bandwidth in Hz and SNR<sub>min</sub> the demodulator's need in dB.
F = 1.413 + 0.143 + 0.077 = 1.632, so NF = 10 log₁₀ 1.632 = 2.13 dB and T<sub>e</sub> = 0.632 × 290 = 183 K. The mixer's 10 dB and the IF stage's 15 dB together add only 0.63 dB to the LNA's 1.5 dB.
Sensitivity: 10 log₁₀(2 × 10⁵) = 53.0 dB, so P<sub>min</sub> = −174 + 53.0 + 2.13 + 9 = −109.9 dBm.
Closing check: the LNA's share of F is 1.413/1.632 = 87 %. If the noise figures were wrongly added in dB, the answer would be 26.5 dB, more than 24 dB too pessimistic.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a superheterodyne receiver and explain the role of the RF filter, LNA, mixer, LO, IF filter and demodulator. Define the image frequency. For an FM receiver tuned to 98.3 MHz with a 10.7 MHz IF and a high-side LO, find the LO, the image and the image rejection of a Q = 40 tuned stage.
outline: antenna → RF filter → LNA → mixer (LO) → IF filter → IF amp → demodulator
IF filter fixed and sharp, sets selectivity; RF filter removes the image

answer.pre:
antenna
  ↓
RF band-pass filter (preselector)
  ↓
LNA
  ↓
mixer  ←  local oscillator (tuned with the RF filter)
  ↓
IF filter (fixed, sharp)
  ↓
IF amplifier
  ↓
demodulator  →  audio

answer: RF filter (preselector): passes the band, attenuates the image and strong out-of-band signals before they reach the active stages.
LNA: adds gain with little noise, so it sets the receiver's noise figure (Friis).

Mixer and LO: the mixer multiplies the RF signal by the LO and produces sum and difference frequencies; the difference is the IF, f<sub>IF</sub> = |f<sub>RF</sub> − f<sub>LO</sub>|. Tuning the LO tunes the receiver.

IF filter and amplifier: the IF never changes, so a sharp ceramic, crystal or SAW filter selects one channel there; the IF amplifier supplies most of the gain. Demodulator: recovers the message (an FM discriminator here).

Image frequency: the other input that gives the same IF, on the far side of the LO: f<sub>si</sub> = 2f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>RF</sub>, which is f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> for a high-side LO. After the mixer it overlaps the wanted channel, so it must be removed before the mixer.
Qρ = 40 × 0.3965 = 15.86; α = √(1 + 15.86²) = √252.5 = 15.9, that is 20 log₁₀ 15.9 = 24.0 dB. Two such tuned stages (RF amplifier input and output) give 48.0 dB.

Why the IF filter, not the RF filter, sets selectivity: FM stations are spaced 200 kHz apart. A filter that passes 200 kHz at 98.3 MHz would need Q ≈ 98.3/0.2 ≈ 490 and would have to retune for every station. At a fixed 10.7 MHz the same bandwidth needs Q ≈ 54, which a ceramic filter provides without tuning.

Choice of IF: a higher IF moves the image further away. With a 45 MHz IF the image would be at 188.3 MHz, ρ = 1.394, and one Q = 40 stage would reject it by 34.9 dB instead of 24.0 dB, but a 200 kHz filter at 45 MHz is harder to make. A double-conversion receiver takes both: a high first IF for the image and a low second IF for the channel.
Closing check: the image is 21.4 MHz above the signal, 2f<sub>IF</sub>, and 2 × 109.0 − 98.3 = 119.7 MHz confirms it.

bank.q: Classify RF power amplifiers A, AB, B and C by conduction angle. For each give the ideal maximum drain efficiency and the linearity, and compute the ideal efficiency of a Class C stage that conducts for 120°.
answer: Conduction angle is the part of the RF cycle, in degrees, during which the transistor carries current; the bias point sets it.

head: Class
Conduction angle
Ideal max η<sub>D</sub>
Linearity and use
rows: Most linear; quiescent current flows always
Good in push-pull; crossover distortion if under-biased
Poor; for constant-envelope FM and CW

answer: Where the numbers come from: Class A draws a constant I<sub>DC</sub> = I<sub>max</sub>/2 and at full swing delivers (V<sub>DD</sub>I<sub>max</sub>/2)/2, half its DC power. In Class B the average current is I<sub>p</sub>/π, so η = (V<sub>DD</sub>I<sub>p</sub>/2)/(V<sub>DD</sub>I<sub>p</sub>/π) = π/4 = 78.5 %.
For a reduced conduction angle α (radians) at full swing: η = (α − sin α)/[4(sin(α/2) − (α/2)cos(α/2))].

The price: for the same peak current the fundamental output falls by 1.1 dB at 120° (2.1 dB at 90°), and the output amplitude no longer follows the input, so Class C cannot amplify AM or OFDM without distortion.

What the efficiency means in watts: for 1 W of RF output an ideal Class A stage draws 1/0.5 = 2.0 W of DC and turns 1.0 W into heat; Class B draws 1/0.785 = 1.27 W and wastes 0.27 W; the 120° Class C stage draws 1/0.897 = 1.12 W and wastes 0.12 W.

Class AB is chosen in practice because a Class B stage biased exactly at cut-off has crossover distortion where one device hands over to the other; a small quiescent current removes it at a small cost in efficiency.
Closing check: the formula gives 0.5 at α = 2π (Class A) and π/4 = 0.785 at α = π (Class B), matching the table.

bank.q: State the Barkhausen criterion. Explain how a VCO tunes and what phase noise means in dBc/Hz. A receiver's 2 GHz LO has −125.6 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset; a −30 dBm blocker sits 1 MHz from a −90 dBm wanted signal in a 200 kHz channel. Find the reciprocal-mixing noise and the resulting SNR.
outline: L(Δf): SSB noise in 1 Hz at Δf ÷ carrier
reciprocal mixing: P<sub>b</sub> + L + 10 log₁₀B = −102.6 dBm
answer: Barkhausen: an amplifier A with feedback β oscillates steadily at the frequency where the loop gain Aβ has magnitude exactly 1 and phase 0° (or a whole number of 360°). At start-up |Aβ| is made 2 to 3 so noise grows; saturation then brings it down to 1.

VCO tuning: an LC tank sets f = 1/(2π√(LC)). A varactor in the tank changes C with the control voltage, so f<sub>out</sub> = f₀ + K<sub>VCO</sub>V<sub>tune</sub>, where K<sub>VCO</sub> (Hz/V) is the slope. A wide range needs a large K<sub>VCO</sub>, which also turns control-line noise into frequency noise.

Phase noise: random phase wander spreads part of the carrier's power to nearby frequencies. L(Δf) is the single-sideband noise power in a 1 Hz band at offset Δf, divided by the carrier power, in dBc/Hz. −125.6 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz means that 1 MHz from the carrier, each hertz holds 125.6 dB less power than the carrier.

Reciprocal mixing: in the mixer the LO's noise skirt multiplies every input. The strong blocker, mixed with the LO's noise 1 MHz from the LO, lands exactly on the IF of the wanted signal, as if the blocker carried that skirt.
Noise added in the 200 kHz channel: P<sub>b</sub> + L(1 MHz) + 10 log₁₀B = −30 − 125.6 + 53.0 = −102.6 dBm.
SNR = −90 − (−102.6) = 12.6 dB, set by the LO, not by the receiver's own noise. For comparison, the thermal floor of a 3 dB-NF receiver in 200 kHz is −174 + 53.0 + 3 = −118.0 dBm, 15.4 dB lower.
To make reciprocal mixing as small as the thermal floor, L(1 MHz) would need to be −118.0 + 30 − 53.0 = −141 dBc/Hz.

Ways to improve it: a VCO with a higher-Q tank or more tank power (Leeson's model gives 6 dB per doubling of Q in the 1/f² region and 3 dB per doubling of power); a sharper RF or IF filter that attenuates the blocker before the mixer; or a frequency plan that keeps the strongest expected blockers further from the channel.
Closing check: adding the two noises, 10 log₁₀(10<sup>−10.26</sup> + 10<sup>−11.80</sup>) = −102.5 dBm, so the SNR is 12.5 dB; the LO term dominates.

bank.q: A receiver has an LNA (G = 15 dB, NF = 2 dB), a mixer (G = 10 dB, NF = 8 dB) and an IF amplifier (G = 20 dB, NF = 6 dB). Find the cascaded noise figure and noise temperature, the sensitivity in 1 MHz for SNR = 10 dB, the effect of a 2 dB filter placed in front of the LNA, and the effect of raising the LNA gain to 20 dB.
outline: filter in front: NF = 4.46 dB, exactly 2 dB worse
answer: Sensitivity in 1 MHz: P<sub>min</sub> = −174 + 60 + 2.46 + 10 = −101.5 dBm.

2 dB filter in front: F<sub>f</sub> = 1.585, G<sub>f</sub> = 1/1.585. F = 1.585 + (1.762 − 1) × 1.585 = 1.585 + 1.208 = 2.793, NF = 4.46 dB: exactly 2 dB worse, and the sensitivity worsens to −99.5 dBm.

Comment: the LNA supplies 1.585/1.762 = 90 % of F. Raising its gain by 5 dB buys only 0.31 dB, while it lowers the cascaded IIP3, so 15 dB is a reasonable choice. Any loss before the LNA must be kept as small as possible.

Noise temperatures of the stages: LNA (1.585 − 1) × 290 = 170 K, mixer (6.310 − 1) × 290 = 1540 K, IF amplifier (3.981 − 1) × 290 = 865 K. The mixer is the noisiest block by far, but divided by G₁ = 31.62 it contributes only 48.7 K.

Where should the 2 dB filter go? Before the LNA it costs the full 2 dB of noise figure but protects the LNA from strong out-of-band signals; after the LNA it adds (1.585 − 1)/31.62 = 0.019 and also raises the mixer and IF terms by 1.585 times, so F = 1.885 and NF = 2.75 dB, only 0.29 dB worse than without it, but the LNA must then survive the blockers on its own. Receivers that face strong nearby transmitters keep a low-loss filter in front; quiet-band receivers put the LNA first.
Sensitivity in other bandwidths: every factor of 10 in B adds 10 dB, so the same chain in 10 MHz has P<sub>min</sub> = −91.5 dBm and in 100 kHz −111.5 dBm.

bank.q: An amplifier has IIP3 = −10 dBm, gain 20 dB and NF = 6 dB in a 1 MHz bandwidth. Find OIP3, the input noise floor, the SFDR and the per-tone input at the top of that range. Check that the IM3 there equals the noise floor, estimate P1dB,in and the blocking dynamic range, and say why SFDR is the smaller of the two.
answer: OIP3 = IIP3 + G = −10 + 20 = 10 dBm.
Input noise floor: N = −174 + 10 log₁₀(10⁶) + 6 = −174 + 60 + 6 = −108 dBm.
Top of the range: the per-tone input at which the input-referred IM3 equals N. From 3P<sub>in</sub> − 2·IIP3 = N: P<sub>in</sub> = (2 × (−10) + (−108))/3 = −128/3 = −42.7 dBm.
Check: IM3 = 3 × (−42.7) − 2 × (−10) = −128 + 20 = −108 dBm, equal to N. At the output: tone = −42.7 + 20 = −22.7 dBm, IM3 = 3(−22.7) − 2(10) = −88 dBm, which is N + G = −88 dBm.
SFDR = P<sub>in,top</sub> − N = −42.7 + 108 = 65.3 dB, the same as step 3.
Compression estimate: for a memoryless cubic, P1dB,in = IIP3 − 9.6 dB = −19.6 dBm. Blocking dynamic range BDR = P1dB,in − N = −19.6 + 108 = 88.4 dB.

Why SFDR is smaller: IM3 rises 3 dB per dB, so it climbs out of the noise floor at −42.7 dBm, 23 dB before the single-tone compression point. SFDR changes by only two-thirds of any change in IIP3 or N: 6 dB more NF would cost 4 dB of SFDR.

Derivation of the SFDR formula: the input-referred IM3 is 3P<sub>in</sub> − 2·IIP3 (slope 3 through the intercept). Setting it equal to N and solving gives P<sub>in</sub> = (2·IIP3 + N)/3, so SFDR = P<sub>in</sub> − N = (2/3)(IIP3 − N).

Distortion at a lower level, for comparison: at −30 dBm per tone the input-referred IM3 is 3(−30) − 2(−10) = −70 dBm, that is 2(P<sub>in</sub> − IIP3) = −40 dBc. Each 1 dB drop of the tones lowers IM3 by 3 dB and improves the dBc figure by 2 dB.

How to raise SFDR: a lower NF lowers N (each 3 dB gives 2 dB of SFDR), a narrower bandwidth lowers N (a 100 kHz channel gives N = −118 dBm and SFDR = 72.0 dB), and a higher IIP3 raises the top (each 3 dB gives 2 dB).
Closing check: (2/3)(98) = 65.33 and −108 + 65.33 = −42.67 dBm; both forms agree.

bank.q: A mixer has RF = 2.1 GHz and LO = 1.8 GHz. Find the IF for down-conversion, the image, and the half-IF spur. Then the same mixer is used to up-convert a 300 MHz IF to 2.1 GHz: give both LO choices and the unwanted sideband for each, and say which filtering is needed.
outline: up-conversion: LO 1.8 GHz (unwanted 1.5 GHz) or 2.4 GHz (unwanted 2.7 GHz)
answer: Down-conversion: f<sub>IF</sub> = |f<sub>RF</sub> − f<sub>LO</sub>| = |2.1 − 1.8| = 0.3 GHz = 300 MHz. The LO is below the RF: a low-side LO.
Image: f<sub>si</sub> = 2f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>RF</sub> = 3.6 − 2.1 = 1.5 GHz. Check: |1.5 − 1.8| = 0.3 GHz. It is 600 MHz (2f<sub>IF</sub>) below the signal, on the other side of the LO.

Half-IF spur: for a low-side LO it lies at f<sub>RF</sub> − f<sub>IF</sub>/2 = 2.1 − 0.15 = 1.95 GHz. Check with m = n = 2: |2 × 1.8 − 2 × 1.95| = |3.6 − 3.9| = 0.3 GHz. It is only 150 MHz from the signal, so the RF filter rejects it much less than the image.

Filtering for reception: an RF band-pass filter centred on 2.1 GHz before the mixer must attenuate 1.5 GHz (image) and 1.95 GHz (half-IF spur); after the mixer an IF filter at 300 MHz removes the sum at 3.9 GHz and LO feedthrough.
Up-conversion of a 300 MHz IF to 2.1 GHz: the mixer gives f<sub>LO</sub> ± f<sub>IF</sub>, so either LO = 2.1 − 0.3 = 1.8 GHz (wanted = sum) or LO = 2.1 + 0.3 = 2.4 GHz (wanted = difference).

In both cases an RF band-pass filter after the mixer passes 2.1 GHz and rejects the unwanted sideband 600 MHz away, and the LO itself (300 MHz away), which leaks through with finite LO-to-RF isolation and is the hardest to filter. A single-sideband (I/Q) up-converter cancels the unwanted sideband in the mixer instead.

Other products at the mixer output when receiving: the sum f<sub>RF</sub> + f<sub>LO</sub> = 3.9 GHz, LO feedthrough at 1.8 GHz and RF feedthrough at 2.1 GHz. All are far from 300 MHz, so a simple IF band-pass or low-pass filter removes them; the hard cases are always the inputs that land exactly on the IF.
Closing check: with LO = 1.8 GHz the same frequency plan serves reception and transmission, since 1.8 + 0.3 = 2.1 and 3.6 − 2.1 = 1.5 GHz.

bank.q: A PA delivers 30 dBm of RF output from 10 W of DC input with 0.5 W of RF drive. Compute the drain efficiency, the PAE, the gain and the heat to be removed. What DC power would a 50 % efficient Class A stage need for the same output, and how much heat would it make?
answer: Convert the output: 30 dBm = 10<sup>30/10</sup> mW = 1000 mW = 1 W.
Drain efficiency: η<sub>D</sub> = P<sub>out</sub>/P<sub>DC</sub> = 1/10 = 0.10 = 10 %.
PAE = (P<sub>out</sub> − P<sub>in</sub>)/P<sub>DC</sub> = (1 − 0.5)/10 = 0.05 = 5 %.
Gain = 10 log₁₀(1/0.5) = 3.0 dB. With so little gain, half of the output was already supplied by the driver, which is why PAE is half of η<sub>D</sub>.

Heat: everything that goes in and does not leave as RF becomes heat: P<sub>diss</sub> = P<sub>DC</sub> + P<sub>in</sub> − P<sub>out</sub> = 10 + 0.5 − 1 = 9.5 W, more than nine times the RF output; it needs a heat sink.
Same 1 W from a Class A stage at its 50 % ideal limit: P<sub>DC</sub> = 1/0.5 = 2 W; heat = 2 + 0.5 − 1 = 1.5 W, about one sixth of the original.

Likely causes of 10 %: heavy back-off (a 10 dB back-off Class A stage runs at 5 %), a wrong load line, or matching loss. Fixes: match the load to R<sub>opt</sub>, choose Class AB or B, and if the signal has a high PAPR use Doherty or envelope tracking.

Ideal Class B for the same 1 W: P<sub>DC</sub> = 1/0.785 = 1.27 W and heat = 1.27 + 0.5 − 1 = 0.77 W. Even ideal classes cannot rescue a stage whose gain is only 3 dB: PAE would be (1 − 0.5)/1.27 = 39 % against η<sub>D</sub> = 78.5 %. More gain per stage (or one more driver stage) is the other half of the fix.
Closing check: energy balance for the given PA, 1 W out + 9.5 W heat = 10.5 W in (10 W DC + 0.5 W drive).

bank.q: A VCO tank uses L = 5 nH (Q = 15 at 2.5 GHz) and an abrupt varactor with C<sub>j0</sub> = 2 pF, φ = 0.7 V, tuned from 1 V to 8 V. Find the tuning range, the average and end-point K<sub>VCO</sub>, and the effect of 0.5 pF of fixed capacitance across the tank. Find the minimum transconductance a cross-coupled pair needs to oscillate at 2.5 GHz.
outline: average K<sub>VCO</sub> = 143 MHz/V; 292 MHz/V at 1 V, 86 MHz/V at 8 V
with 0.5 pF fixed: 1.69 to 2.18 GHz, 70 MHz/V
answer: Varactor: C(V<sub>R</sub>) = C<sub>j0</sub>/√(1 + V<sub>R</sub>/φ). At 1 V: 2/√2.429 = 1.283 pF. At 8 V: 2/√12.43 = 0.567 pF.

Frequencies, f = 1/(2π√(LC)): with 1.283 pF, f = 1/(2π√(6.415 × 10⁻²¹)) = 1.99 GHz; with 0.567 pF, f = 1/(2π√(2.835 × 10⁻²¹)) = 2.99 GHz. The tuning range is 1.99 to 2.99 GHz, a ratio of 1.50 = √(1.283/0.567).
Average K<sub>VCO</sub> = (2.99 − 1.99) GHz/(8 − 1) V = 1.00 GHz/7 V = 143 MHz/V.

K<sub>VCO</sub> is not constant: by differentiating numerically (a 10 mV step) it is 292 MHz/V near 1 V and 86 MHz/V near 8 V, because C(V) changes fastest at low bias. The PLL's loop gain therefore changes by a factor of 3.4 across the band.

answer.text: Adding 0.5 pF of fixed capacitance (transistor and layout parasitics):

answer: With the fixed capacitance the range shrinks to 1.69 to 2.18 GHz (ratio 1.29) and the average K<sub>VCO</sub> falls to 0.49 GHz/7 V = 70 MHz/V. Fixed capacitance always cuts the tuning range, which is why VCO layouts keep parasitics small and add switched capacitor banks for coverage.
Tank loss at 2.5 GHz: ωL = 2π × 2.5 × 10⁹ × 5 × 10⁻⁹ = 78.5 Ω, so R<sub>p</sub> = QωL = 15 × 78.5 = 1178 Ω.

A cross-coupled pair presents −2/g<sub>m</sub> across the tank. Oscillation needs 2/g<sub>m</sub> ≤ R<sub>p</sub>, so g<sub>m</sub> ≥ 2/1178 = 1.70 mS. Designers use 2 to 3 times this, about 4 to 5 mS, for reliable start-up (Barkhausen loop gain 2 to 3).

Why the large K<sub>VCO</sub> near 1 V matters: noise on the control line of 10 nV/√Hz becomes frequency noise K<sub>VCO</sub> × 10 nV/√Hz, and its phase noise at offset f<sub>m</sub> is (K<sub>VCO</sub>v<sub>n</sub>)²/(2f<sub>m</sub>²). At 1 MHz offset that is −113.7 dBc/Hz with 292 MHz/V and −124.3 dBc/Hz with 86 MHz/V: at the low-bias end the control line, not the tank, would set the phase noise.

bank.q: A direct-conversion receiver uses a 2.4 GHz LO at 0 dBm with 60 dB of LO-to-RF isolation and 30 dB of gain before baseband; the wanted signal is −90 dBm. Analyse three mechanisms that put unwanted energy at DC, with numbers: LO self-mixing, second-order distortion from a −30 dBm blocker with IIP2 = +40 dBm, and flicker noise with a 1 MHz corner across a 100 kHz channel. Give a fix for each.
outline: LO leakage −60 dBm at the input, self-mixes to a DC offset 30 dB above the wanted signal at baseband
IM2 = 2P<sub>b</sub> − IIP2 = −100 dBm, only 10 dB below the wanted
flicker: average noise density 16.8 dB above white over 1 to 100 kHz
fixes: calibration and AC coupling, higher IIP2 (balanced mixers, trimming), chopping or a high-pass corner
answer: Setting: zero-IF, so the channel occupies DC to 100 kHz at baseband on I and Q. Anything that appears at or near DC lands on the signal.

LO self-mixing: LO leakage at the RF port = 0 − 60 = −60 dBm. It travels to the LNA input (or the antenna and back) and is amplified and mixed with the LO, giving a DC term. Referred to the input it is −60 dBm, 30 dB above the −90 dBm wanted signal; after the 30 dB of gain it is −30 dBm of DC against −60 dBm of signal. A DC offset that large can saturate the baseband amplifiers and ADC.

Fix: offset cancellation loops or a one-time DC calibration, AC coupling with a corner of a few kilohertz (a narrow notch at DC costs little for wideband OFDM), and better LO-to-RF isolation through balanced layout.

Second-order distortion: a strong amplitude-varying blocker x(t)² produces a baseband term. Input-referred, IM2 = 2P<sub>b</sub> − IIP2 = 2(−30) − 40 = −100 dBm, only 10 dB below the −90 dBm wanted signal. If the demodulator needs 15 dB SNR this already fails.
Fix: raise IIP2. With IIP2 = +50 dBm, IM2 = −110 dBm (20 dB below the signal). Balanced (differential) LNA and mixer circuits cancel even-order terms; IIP2 calibration trims the remaining mismatch.

Flicker noise: with a 1 MHz corner, the noise density is (1 + f<sub>c</sub>/f) times the white level. Averaged over 1 kHz to 100 kHz this factor is 47.5, that is 16.8 dB above white noise. A 3 dB receiver noise figure becomes far worse inside the channel.

Fix: large-area or bipolar baseband devices to lower f<sub>c</sub>, chopper stabilisation, more gain before the mixer so baseband flicker is referred to the input over a larger gain, or a low-IF plan. A 10 kHz high-pass corner alone cuts the average factor to 26.6 (14.2 dB).
I/Q mismatch is a fourth problem: it does not add DC, but it leaves the image of the channel's other half (IRR ≈ 4/(ε² + θ²), about 40 dB for 1 % and 1°).
Closing check: 2(−30) − 40 = −100 dBm and 2(−30) − 50 = −110 dBm, 10 dB apart for 10 dB more IIP2, as the slope of 2 for IM2 against the blocker's 1 requires.

bank.q: Compare superheterodyne, direct-conversion and image-reject (Hartley) receivers on image rejection, DC offset, selectivity, integration and power, using the numbers of a 900 MHz receiver (45 MHz IF, Q = 50 preselector) and a Hartley stage with 2 % and 2° mismatch. Recommend one for a low-cost narrowband sensor at 868 MHz and justify it.
outline: superhet: filter-based image rejection, 19.6 dB per Q = 50 stage at 45 MHz IF; excellent selectivity from a SAW IF filter; external filters
zero-IF: no image filter, DC offset, IIP2, flicker, I/Q mismatch; fully integrated
Hartley: IRR ≈ 4/(ε² + θ²) = 33.9 dB; combine with a preselector
recommend low-IF or Hartley with a modest preselector for the sensor

head: Feature
Superheterodyne
Direct conversion
Hartley image-reject
rows: Filters: 19.6 dB per Q = 50 stage at a 45 MHz IF; 80 dB needs a SAW image filter
No separate image; I/Q mismatch leaves a residual of ~30 to 40 dB
Small if the IF is above the flicker corner
Excellent: fixed SAW or crystal IF filter
Poor: external image and IF filters
Good: needs matched I/Q paths and a 90° shifter
More stages and LO power; costly filters

answer: Superheterodyne image rejection with the numbers: f<sub>si</sub> = 990 MHz, ρ = 0.1909, α = √(1 + (50 × 0.1909)²) = 9.60 = 19.6 dB per tuned stage. A −20 dBm image against a −80 dBm signal needs 80 dB of rejection, so either five such stages or a dedicated image filter; this is the main cost of the architecture.

Direct conversion avoids the image filter completely and integrates fully, which is why phones and Wi-Fi use it, but it must fight DC offsets from LO leakage, even-order distortion of blockers and flicker noise. It needs calibration loops and, for narrowband signals, suffers most: a 12.5 kHz channel sits entirely inside the flicker region.

Hartley: ε = 0.02, θ = 0.0349 rad, ε² + θ² = 0.00162, IRR ≈ 2470 = 33.9 dB. Alone this is not enough for an 80 dB requirement, but with a modest preselector it adds: at a 10.7 MHz IF a Q = 50 stage gives 8.1 dB, total 42.0 dB; calibration that reaches 0.5 % and 0.5° gives IRR ≈ 4/(0.000025 + 0.000076) = 39 500 = 46 dB.

The low-IF receiver is the practical hybrid: quadrature down-conversion to a few hundred kilohertz, so the channel avoids DC and flicker, with the image (the adjacent channel on the other side) rejected by the I/Q processing at 30 to 50 dB. Because the image is an adjacent channel of similar strength, that is usually enough.

Recommendation for an 868 MHz narrowband sensor (kilohertz-wide channel, battery powered, low cost): a low-IF receiver with polyphase (Hartley-type) image rejection and a fixed SAW band filter at the antenna.

Justification: (1) the narrow channel would sit in the flicker region of a zero-IF design, so low-IF avoids the worst zero-IF problem; (2) no tunable or external IF filter is needed, so it integrates on one chip like zero-IF; (3) the image is an adjacent channel in the same band, which 35 to 45 dB of IRR handles; (4) the band filter removes out-of-band blockers, protecting the LNA.
A classic superheterodyne would give the best selectivity, but its external filters and second LO cost power and area that a sensor cannot afford.

Power: the superheterodyne needs an LO, an IF amplifier chain and often a second LO, and its external filters need 50 Ω drivers. The zero-IF and low-IF receivers drive only on-chip loads at baseband, which is why they dominate battery-powered radios.
Closing check: 19.6 dB per stage × 5 = 98 dB ≥ 80 dB for the superheterodyne; 33.9 + 8.1 = 42.0 dB for the Hartley design at 10.7 MHz; both numbers come from α = √(1 + Q²ρ²) and IRR ≈ 4/(ε² + θ²).

bank.q: An LNA with NF = 2 dB and IIP3 = 0 dBm drives a mixer with NF = 10 dB and IIP3 = +5 dBm, in a 10 MHz channel. Analyse how the LNA gain sets the noise figure, the cascaded IIP3 and the SFDR for G = 10, 15 and 20 dB, and recommend a gain.
outline: choose about 12 to 15 dB: sensitivity versus blocking
answer: Noise: F = F₁ + (F₂ − 1)/G, with F₁ = 10<sup>0.2</sup> = 1.585 and F₂ = 10 (10 dB). The mixer's term 9/G shrinks as G rises.

Linearity: 1/IIP3 = 1/IIP3₁ + G/IIP3₂ in milliwatts, with IIP3₁ = 1 mW (0 dBm) and IIP3₂ = 3.162 mW (+5 dBm). The mixer's term G/3.162 grows as G rises, because the mixer sees the signal after the LNA's gain.
Dynamic range: N = −174 + 10 log₁₀(10⁷) + NF = −104 + NF dBm, and SFDR = (2/3)(IIP3 − N).

Reading the table: from 10 to 20 dB of gain the noise figure improves by 1.71 dB, but the IIP3 falls by 8.9 dB and the SFDR by 4.8 dB. The gain buys sensitivity with diminishing returns (1.23 dB for the first 5 dB, 0.48 dB for the next 5 dB), while it costs linearity almost dB for dB once the mixer dominates the IIP3 sum.

Blocking: a strong out-of-band signal that the band filter does not remove is amplified by G before the mixer, so the mixer compresses first. At G = 20 dB the cascaded P1dB,in is roughly −15.1 − 9.6 = −24.7 dBm; at G = 10 dB, about −15.8 dBm, a 9 dB difference in the blocker the receiver can tolerate.

Recommendation: about 12 to 15 dB. At 15 dB the noise figure is within 0.48 dB of the 20 dB case, while the IIP3 and SFDR are 4.7 dB and 2.8 dB better. If the radio must survive strong blockers (a phone next to its own transmitter), lean towards 12 dB; if it receives weak signals in a quiet band (GPS), lean towards 20 dB.

Other ways out of the trade: a mixer with a higher IIP3 (a passive mixer at +15 dBm would raise the G = 20 dB cascade to 1/(1 + 100/31.62) = 0.240 mW = −6.2 dBm), a filter between the LNA and the mixer to remove out-of-band blockers before the mixer sees them, or switchable LNA gain, high for weak signals and low when a blocker appears.

Closing check: in the G = 15 dB case the two IIP3 terms are 1 and 10 mW⁻¹, so the mixer causes 91 % of the distortion, while in the noise sum the LNA causes 1.585/1.870 = 85 % of the noise: the two limits sit in opposite stages, which is the whole trade.

bank.q: A transmitter must send an OFDM signal with 8 dB PAPR while meeting its ACLR. Evaluate back-off, digital predistortion, feedforward, Doherty and envelope tracking against linearity, efficiency and complexity, using the ideal Class A and Class B efficiencies at 8 dB back-off.
outline: 8 dB back-off: Class A 7.9 %, Class B 31.3 %
DPD: digital inverse with memory, needs feedback receiver
feedforward: wideband and very linear, poor efficiency
Doherty: peak efficiency at 6 dB back-off
choice: Doherty + DPD for base station, ET + DPD for handset
answer: The problem: peaks 8 dB above the average must not clip, otherwise spectral regrowth lowers the ACLR. A plain PA must therefore run its average 8 dB below its maximum.

Back-off alone: Class A efficiency falls with the power ratio, η = 50 % × 10<sup>−0.8</sup> = 7.9 %; ideal Class B falls with the amplitude ratio, η = 78.5 % × 10<sup>−0.4</sup> = 31.3 %. Linear and simple, but most of the DC power becomes heat.

Digital predistortion (DPD): baseband applies the inverse of the PA's AM-AM and AM-PM curves, with memory terms, so the PA can run close to compression (back-off of a few dB beyond the PAPR rather than more). It needs a feedback receiver and adaptation, which cost power and silicon, but it is now standard because the gain in PA efficiency is larger.

Feedforward: the error between the PA output and a clean copy of the input is amplified by a second amplifier and subtracted through couplers. It cancels distortion over a wide band with very high linearity, but the error amplifier, delay lines and couplers lose power, so overall efficiency is low (often near that of plain back-off). It suits multi-carrier amplifiers where linearity is paramount.

Doherty: carrier and peaking amplifiers with a quarter-wave inverter keep the efficiency near its peak at 6 dB back-off (ideal 78.5 % with Class B-biased devices) and above Class B down to about 8 to 10 dB. It is analog, narrowband (the inverter) and somewhat nonlinear, so it is almost always paired with DPD.

Envelope tracking (ET): the supply follows the envelope, so the transistor's voltage headroom is small at every instant and efficiency stays high through the back-off range. It needs a fast, efficient supply modulator whose bandwidth must exceed the signal's envelope bandwidth, and timing alignment between envelope and RF.

head: Method
Linearity
Efficiency at 8 dB PAPR
Complexity
Typical use
rows: Lets the PA run near compression

answer: Verdict: for a base station, a GaN Doherty PA with DPD gives the best efficiency with ACLR met; for a handset, envelope tracking with DPD, because a Doherty inverter is hard to make wideband across many phone bands. Pure back-off is acceptable only at low power, where the wasted heat is small.

Ideal Doherty at 8 dB back-off: the amplitude ratio is v = 10<sup>−8/20</sup> = 0.398, below the 0.5 transition, so only the carrier amplifier works, at η = 78.5 % × 2v = 62.5 %, twice the 31.3 % of plain Class B.
Closing check: 10<sup>−0.8</sup> = 0.158 and 10<sup>−0.4</sup> = 0.398, so 50 % × 0.158 = 7.9 % and 78.5 % × 0.398 = 31.3 %, a factor of 4 between the classes.

bank.q: A 2 GHz synthesizer (N = 200, 10 MHz reference at −155 dBc/Hz beyond 10 kHz) drives the mixer of a receiver that must tolerate a −30 dBm blocker 1 MHz from a −90 dBm signal in a 200 kHz channel and needs 10 dB SNR. The free VCO follows Leeson's model with −103.0 dBc/Hz at 100 kHz and −125.6 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz. Evaluate loop bandwidths of 50 kHz, 180 kHz and 1 MHz for phase noise, reciprocal mixing and lock time.
outline: 180 kHz is the crossover: lowest noise
1 MHz loop: noise at 1 MHz ≈ −109 dBc/Hz, reciprocal mixing −86 dBm, fails
50 kHz or 180 kHz: −125.6 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz, SNR 12.6 dB, passes
lock time a few 1/f<sub>L</sub>: 180 kHz faster than 50 kHz
answer: Reference at the output: −155 + 20 log₁₀200 = −155 + 46.0 = −109.0 dBc/Hz beyond 10 kHz. Inside the loop bandwidth the output follows this; outside, it follows the free VCO.
Requirement at 1 MHz: reciprocal-mixing noise = −30 + L(1 MHz) + 10 log₁₀(2 × 10⁵) = −30 + L + 53.0. For SNR ≥ 10 dB this must be ≤ −100 dBm, so L(1 MHz) ≤ −123.0 dBc/Hz.

answer.text: Output phase noise for each loop bandwidth (approximating the loop as a sharp switch between the two sources):

answer: 50 kHz: the 1 MHz offset is far outside the loop, so the blocker test passes with 12.6 dB SNR (2.6 dB margin). But between 50 and 180 kHz the free VCO (−103 dBc/Hz at 100 kHz) is up to 6 dB worse than the reference, so the integrated phase noise in the channel and the EVM are worse.

180 kHz: the loop bandwidth sits where the VCO and the multiplied reference cross (about 176 kHz). Close-in noise is the −109.0 dBc/Hz floor, and the 1 MHz value is still the VCO's −125.6 dBc/Hz: the blocker test passes with the same 12.6 dB, and the integrated noise is the lowest of the three.

1 MHz: the loop now copies the multiplied reference out to 1 MHz, where it is about −109 dBc/Hz, 16.6 dB worse than the VCO. Reciprocal mixing becomes −30 − 109 + 53.0 = −86 dBm, 4 dB above the wanted signal: the receiver fails the blocker test.

Lock time: roughly a few times 1/f<sub>L</sub>, so about 20 µs per time constant at 50 kHz, 5.6 µs at 180 kHz and 1 µs at 1 MHz. The 1 MHz loop locks fastest but fails on noise; 180 kHz is more than three times faster than 50 kHz and passes.

Verdict: choose about 180 kHz. It gives the lowest integrated phase noise, meets the blocker requirement with 2.6 dB of margin, and locks faster than the 50 kHz design. For more margin, improve the VCO (higher Q, more tank power) rather than narrowing the loop: doubling the tank power gives 3 dB at 1 MHz.

The required phase noise also fixes the VCO design: with Leeson's model, L(1 MHz) ≤ −123.0 dBc/Hz leaves only 2.6 dB of slack, so the tank Q (8) and power (1 mW) cannot be relaxed, and the loop bandwidth must stay well below 1 MHz so that offset remains in the VCO-dominated region.

glossary.def: Power in dB relative to 1 mW: P(dBm) = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW); 0 dBm = 1 mW.
2π × energy stored ÷ energy lost per cycle; for a series model |X|/R.
The frequency where a part's parasitic reactance cancels its main reactance; above it an inductor looks capacitive.
A reverse-biased junction or MOS capacitor whose capacitance is set by a DC voltage.
F = SNR<sub>in</sub>/SNR<sub>out</sub> with the source at 290 K; a linear ratio.
NF = 10 log₁₀F, the SNR degradation of a stage in dB.
T<sub>e</sub> = (F − 1) × 290 K, the input noise temperature that accounts for a stage's own noise.
The weakest input that gives the demodulator its required SNR.
The fall of gain at high input; P1dB is where it reaches 1 dB.
New tones made when two or more tones pass through a nonlinear stage, such as 2f₁ − f₂.
Input third-order intercept: the extrapolated input where the fundamental and IM3 lines meet.
Spurious-free dynamic range: from the noise floor to the input at which IM3 reaches the noise floor.
A receiver that converts the RF signal to a fixed IF for filtering and gain before demodulation.
The unwanted input that mixes to the same IF as the wanted signal: f<sub>si</sub> = 2f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>RF</sub>.
A zero-IF receiver that mixes straight to baseband I and Q.
Conversion gain for the wanted signal ÷ conversion gain for the image, in dB.
A pair of band filters that lets an FDD transmitter and receiver share one antenna.
Effective isotropic radiated power: transmit power at the antenna plus antenna gain in dBi.
Adjacent-channel leakage ratio: wanted-channel power ÷ adjacent-channel power, in dB.
Low-noise amplifier: the first gain stage, which sets the receiver noise figure.
A source inductor that gives an LNA a noiseless real input resistance ω<sub>T</sub>L<sub>s</sub>.
A mixer's output power at the wanted frequency ÷ its input signal power.
An input frequency other than the wanted one that some product m·f<sub>LO</sub> ± n·f<sub>RF</sub> moves to the IF.
Power-added efficiency: (P<sub>out</sub> − P<sub>in</sub>)/P<sub>DC</sub>.
How far, in dB, a PA's average output sits below its maximum or compressed output.
A carrier and a peaking amplifier joined by a quarter-wave inverter to keep efficiency high at back-off.
L(Δf): single-sideband noise in 1 Hz at offset Δf ÷ carrier power, in dBc/Hz.
Phase-locked loop: locks a VCO to N times a reference frequency.
A strong blocker mixing with the LO's phase-noise skirt onto the wanted signal's IF.
